data: SMD 0.86 SD lower (1.59 lower to 0.13 lower)

The evidence for balance is very uncertain. One trial contributes. In taekwondo athletes with flexible flatfoot, the Biodex overall stability index at 12 weeks was 0.93 with an orthosis and 1.46 without one ( g = −0.859, P = 0.02). The post‐test was performed barefoot with the orthosis removed, so this is an adaptation effect after 12 weeks of wear rather than the effect of the device while it is worn. No consensus minimal clinically important difference exists for this index, and none of the included studies measured falls, injuries, or activity limitation directly.

No single estimate Region‐specific SMDs range from 1.93 SD lower at the second metatarsal (2.68 lower to 1.18 lower) to 1.76 SD higher at the medial midfoot (1.05 higher to 2.46 higher); all eight regions are given in Table 1

Orthoses redistribute plantar load rather than lowering it uniformly. Loading fell at the second metatarsal, at the third‐to‐fifth metatarsals, and at the heel, and rose at the medial midfoot and the lateral toe, which is the mechanical effect a medial arch support is designed to produce. A single averaged figure would set these reductions against the increases and approach zero, concealing the redistribution, so none is reported. The evidence is very uncertain: One small study that did not randomize allocation contributes, and no study in this review related the size or the direction of pressure change to change in symptoms.
SMD 1.02 SD lower (1.54 lower to 0.49 lower)

The evidence for pain reduction is very uncertain. One trial contributes. On its designated primary outcome, a 100 mm pain visual analog scale at 8 weeks, orthoses were 1.02 standard deviations better than a sham insole ( P < 0.001), a between‐group difference of 18.95 mm that approaches but does not reach the predefined minimal clinically important difference of 20 mm. The estimate is not robust to the choice of instrument within that same trial: Its foot function index total gives g = −0.28, a small effect. The pain conclusion of this review therefore rests on a single instrument choice within a single trial, and it should not be read as a stable estimate of how much orthoses reduce pain.
SMD 0.97 SD lower (1.62 lower to 0.33 lower)

This row does not estimate the effect of an orthosis. Both arms wore the identical prefabricated insole and only one performed short foot exercises, so the contrast is the added effect of the exercise program: 2.3 versus 3.2 points on a 0‐10 scale at 6 weeks ( P = 0.003), a difference of 0.9 points, below the predefined 2‐point threshold. It is reported in a separate row rather than combined with the row above. That separation is not costless, and the pooled figure it forgoes is reported in full in the results; it is kept separate anyway, because a contrast in which both arms wore the orthosis cannot contribute to an estimate of what the orthosis does.
